Kuwait went to Islamabad and signed a new military cooperation pact with Pakistan. Saudi Arabia sent a senior security delegation to Baghdad for border-control and intelligence talks. The region is buying insurance before the next crisis sends the premium through the roof.

Kuwait’s defense minister, Sheikh Abdullah Ali Abdullah Al-Salem Al-Sabah, signed the agreement with Pakistani Defense Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif. It builds on a 2023 pact and covers training, capacity-building, border management, operational coordination and military readiness. Kuwait is not replacing the U.S. security umbrella. It is adding a backup generator.

In Baghdad, Saudi and Iraqi officials discussed tighter control of their shared border and more intelligence sharing. 

Iraqi delegations had visited Riyadh earlier this month, while Saudi intelligence chief Khalid bin Ali Al-Humaidan met Iraq’s prime minister in Baghdad. 

Iraq says it will not allow its territory to be used for attacks on other countries. That sentence becomes more valuable each time it is repeated.

Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf welcomed the withdrawal of U.S.-led coalition forces from Iraq as a “historic achievement” for Iraqis. Washington still has a military footprint in the country, but its partners are building side channels while Tehran celebrates the shrinking of the old order.

The Gulf once outsourced regional security to Washington. Now Kuwait is calling Pakistan, Saudi Arabia is calling Baghdad, Qatar is calling Tehran, and every capital is keeping a second phone.

Israel should read the directory carefully. These agreements do not form an anti-Israel alliance. They do show that the region is preparing for a future in which U.S. guarantees arrive late, with conditions attached.

The Sanctions Choir

Washington announced an “economic onslaught” against Iran. China, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and France replied with the diplomatic version of earplugs.

China said its trade with Iran complies with international law and opposed unilateral U.S. sanctions lacking United Nations authorization. Qatar also called the measures unilateral while saying it remains in contact with both Washington and Tehran to revive negotiations. Beijing wants its oil flows protected. Doha wants the strait open long enough to keep everyone paid.

France and Saudi Arabia used gentler language, which is what countries do when their banks, oil markets and security arrangements are all in the room. 

Emmanuel Macron and Mohammed bin Salman called for a negotiated settlement on Iran’s nuclear program. They urged Tehran to resume full cooperation with the International Atomic Energy Agency. They also demanded normal shipping in Hormuz, with no tolls or restrictions.

The Houthis provided the blunt translation. Deputy Foreign Minister Abdulwahid Abu Ras called the sanctions “psychological war” after the failure of the military option. He warned regional governments not to become U.S. “tools” against Iran.

Tehran’s allies say sanctions are useless theater. They also demand that the theater close immediately. China calls the sanctions illegal. Qatar calls them unilateral. Riyadh and Paris call for diplomacy. The Houthis call them a failed war.

Nobody is arguing that pressure does nothing. They are arguing over who gets to control it.

The U.S. sanctions Iran to force a deal. Iran’s friends oppose the sanctions to force a deal. Diplomacy has become a hostage exchange where every side claims to hold the key.
